appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Micro-batches now in depth: the unbounded-table model, lazy `readStream`, `processingTime` vs `availableNow` triggers, and what happens when a batch takes longer than its trigger (backlog, not parallel batches) — see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, sections 1–4.

appendExercises.q: If a micro-batch takes 12 s but the trigger is every 5 s, Spark runs the overdue micro-batches in parallel to keep up.
appendExercises.explain: No. In the normal micro-batch model batches run **sequentially**: the next starts after the current one finishes, so a processing backlog builds and latency grows. That's a signal that ingestion rate > processing capacity.

appendFlashcards.q: Trigger 5 s, micro-batch needs 12 s — what happens?
appendFlashcards.a: Batches stay sequential → backlog builds, latency grows (ingest > capacity).

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: The streaming engine can itself run **batch + incremental**: `writeStream.trigger(availableNow=True)` on a schedule processes only what's new since the checkpoint, then stops — no hand-written `last_processed_timestamp`. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 4.

appendExercises.q: An hourly job uses `readStream` + `writeStream.trigger(availableNow=True)` with a checkpoint. How do you classify it?
options: Scheduled (batch-like) + incremental, using the streaming engine
appendExercises.explain: It runs on a schedule and stops (batch-like execution) but touches only new input thanks to the checkpoint (incremental). AvailableNow = scheduled incremental processing with streaming semantics, not an always-on stream.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Open the box: a checkpoint holds **offsets/** (what each micro-batch reads), **commits/** (what reached the sink), **state/** (stateful operators) and **metadata** (query identity) — not just 'the last offset'. Why new code can make it incompatible, and why deleting it means a brand-new query: see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 9.

appendExercises.q: Certification trap: what does a Structured Streaming checkpoint store?
options: Offsets, commits, query metadata and state (where applicable)
A full copy of the sink table
appendExercises.explain: Offsets/progress, commit information, query metadata and — for stateful queries — state. 'Just the last timestamp' is the classic wrong answer; that's why deleting it loses progress **and** state and turns the next run into a new query.

appendFlashcards.a: offsets/, commits/, state/ (stateful), metadata — the query's identity and memory.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Streaming FROM a Delta table is append-oriented: if the source gets UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE, read its **Change Data Feed** (`readChangeFeed`) to propagate row-level changes, or deliberately skip them (`skipChangeCommits`). see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 12.

appendExercises.q: A Silver Delta table receives MERGE updates. A downstream stream must see those row-level changes. What should it read?
appendExercises.explain: A plain `readStream.table(...)` on Delta is append-oriented and fails (or, with skipChangeCommits, ignores) commits that change existing rows. The Change Data Feed exposes inserts/updates/deletes as a stream.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: For streams, 'no new data' has a 9-point checklist: query active? source producing? new offsets? checkpoint corrupted? sink blocked? state batch stuck? executor failure? permission expired? source retention violated? — and **don't restart blindly**. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 15 (playbook 'Stream stopped making progress').

appendExercises.q: When a streaming query stops making progress, the safest first move is to restart it with a fresh checkpoint location.
appendExercises.explain: No. First inspect `query.status`/`lastProgress` and walk the checklist. A new checkpoint makes the query brand new → reprocessing and duplicates, and a restart can destroy the evidence.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Exactly-once has edges: Delta sinks are exactly-once, but a **non-idempotent foreachBatch** (emails, `balance += x`) replays on retry, and **source duplicates** pass straight through (processing guarantee ≠ business dedup). Bounded streaming dedup: `withWatermark(...).dropDuplicates(["event_id", "event_time"])`. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, sections 10 & 13.

appendExercises.q: A streaming job writes to Delta (exactly-once sink) AND posts each order to a CRM inside foreachBatch. After a crash, the CRM shows order 123 twice; Delta doesn't. Most likely cause?
options: The retried batch re-ran a non-idempotent external side effect
appendExercises.explain: The retried micro-batch re-invoked foreachBatch, and the CRM call isn't covered by Delta/checkpoint transactions. Exactly-once stops at non-transactional edges — make the side effect idempotent (business key/version).

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Lazy evaluation applies to streams too: `spark.readStream...load()` only builds a plan; the query starts at `writeStream ... toTable()/start()`. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 2.

appendExercises.explain: No — like any transformation it defines a (streaming) plan. Execution begins when a streaming sink is started with `writeStream ... toTable()` or `.start()`.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → VACUUM breaks stopped streams
appendBlocks.text: VACUUM vs **streaming readers**: a stream reading this table that stays stopped longer than retention may find its needed files vacuumed and fail with a missing-file error. Never 'fix' it with `spark.sql.files.ignoreMissingFiles=true` (silent wrong results) — increase retention or rebuild the stream. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 12.

appendExercises.q: A stream reading `ecommerce.bronze.events` (VACUUM retention 7 days, VACUUM runs daily) was stopped for 2 weeks. On restart it fails: files for a version the checkpoint needs are missing.

options.text: VACUUM removed files the stopped stream still needed
options.fb: Right — the checkpoint points at version X, whose files are gone.
Checkpoints don't expire; the source files did.

options.text: Recover/rebuild the stream and increase retention for the future

options.fb: Databricks warns it can silently produce incorrect results.

options.text: Run VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS to clean up

appendExercises.explain: Streams must run at least once within the source retention window. Design retention and stream operations together.

appendPitfalls.title: VACUUM vs stopped streams
appendPitfalls.text: A stream stopped longer than the source retention can't catch up once its files are vacuumed.
appendPitfalls.fix: Run streams at least once per retention window; increase retention; never use ignoreMissingFiles as a workaround.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: MERGE in a stream: `writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert)` where `upsert(batch_df, batch_id)` runs `DeltaTable.forName(...).merge(...).whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()` — the classic streaming upsert, and the way to get update-like results into Delta (the Delta sink has no update mode). Keep it idempotent: a retried batch may run twice. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 13.

appendExercises.explain: foreachBatch hands each micro-batch to a function as a batch DataFrame, so batch-only MERGE becomes possible; MERGE by key keeps a replayed batch idempotent.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Streaming is a small-file factory: every tiny micro-batch commits small files (1–3 MB each). OPTIMIZE / predictive optimization can compact later, but pick a sensible trigger latency. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, section 14.

appendExercises.q: A stream writes to Delta with `trigger(processingTime="1 second")` although the dashboard refreshes every 15 minutes. DESCRIBE DETAIL shows 400,000 files of ~1 MB. Best first change?
options: Lengthen the trigger to match the real latency need, then OPTIMIZE
appendExercises.explain: Tiny micro-batches mean more scheduling overhead, more commits, more storage API calls and smaller files. Matching the trigger to the real latency need (or AvailableNow on a schedule) attacks the cause; OPTIMIZE then cleans up the existing layout.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Every micro-batch is a Spark job, so skew/spill/shuffle diagnosis applies unchanged — plus a deadline: the batch must finish before the next trigger. Streaming adds **state** (growth, watermark, state store) and **source/sink** (throughput, API latency, storage) branches to the debugging tree; compare `inputRowsPerSecond` vs `processedRowsPerSecond` before CPU. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, sections 14–15.

appendExercises.q: A streaming micro-batch has 100 partitions: 99 finish in 2 s, one skewed partition takes 30 s. The trigger is 5 s. What is the minimum duration of each micro-batch in seconds?
appendExercises.explain: The stage ends with its slowest task → ≥ 30 s, six times the trigger, so backlog grows every batch. Adding workers doesn't split one partition; fix the skew/key design.

appendFlashcards.q: Streaming-specific branches of the debugging tree?
appendFlashcards.a: State (growth, watermark, state store) and Source/Sink (throughput, API latency, storage) — on top of Spark shuffle/skew/spill/join.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Phase 5 is now a full chapter: triggers incl. AvailableNow and serverless rules, stateless vs stateful, event time and windows, watermarks, output modes (Delta sink: append + complete only), checkpoint internals, exactly-once boundaries, joins, foreachBatch + MERGE, 11 debugging playbooks and the Phase 5 mini-project — see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming.

appendBlocks.title: Nuance → Delta sink & serverless triggers
appendBlocks.text: Two corrections to remember for the preview above: the **update** output mode is not supported by the Delta sink (use foreachBatch + MERGE), and a `processingTime` trigger is not supported on serverless notebooks/jobs (use AvailableNow, or a Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode for always-on).

appendExercises.q: The Delta streaming sink supports all three output modes: append, update and complete.
appendExercises.explain: No — append and complete only. Update-like semantics into Delta are built with foreachBatch + MERGE.

appendExercises.q: The preview's code uses `.trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")`. You run it as a serverless job. What happens / what should you use?
options: Works the same as on classic
Not supported on serverless — use availableNow on a schedule, or Lakeflow continuous mode for always-on
Serverless silently converts it to real-time mode
appendExercises.explain: Serverless notebooks/jobs support AvailableNow (and deprecated Once), not time-based ProcessingTime or real-time triggers. Schedule an AvailableNow job, or use a Lakeflow pipeline in continuous mode for an always-on stream.

appendBlocks.title: Level-up → Structured Streaming
appendBlocks.text: Why Phase 6 follows Phase 5: always-running serverless streams are best built as **Lakeflow pipelines in continuous mode**, and recomputation when dimensions change fits declarative/materialized patterns better than a long-running stream-static join. see Chapter 13: Structured Streaming, sections 4 & 11.

appendExercises.q: In a long-running stream-static join, updating the dimension table automatically recomputes all previously written enriched rows.
appendExercises.explain: No. New micro-batches may join against the newer dimension, but already-written outputs are not recomputed. If correctness requires recomputation, materialized/declarative pipeline patterns (Phase 6) are often a better fit.
